p01-feasible-title.name: p01-feasible-title
p01-feasible-title.text: What does "the data can be separated" really mean? Treat each v as a point in the plane

p01-feasible-ctx.name: p01-feasible-ctx
p01-feasible-ctx.text: Four points: positive $(-1,0),(0,1)$, negative $(0,-1),(1,0)$. To be drawable, look only at the slice $b=0$: each $(w_1,w_2)$ is a boundary through the origin.

p01-feasible-src.name: p01-feasible-src
p01-feasible-src.text: Source: The four-point example from the lecture's "prerequisite notation"; the $b=0$ slice and $\mathbf v^{\ast}=(-1,2,0)$ are teaching choices to make the premise "a feasible $\mathbf v^{\ast}$ exists" visible.

p01-feasible-c0.name: p01-feasible-c0
p01-feasible-c0.text: The proof starts by assuming the training data is strictly linearly separable, that is some $\mathbf v^{\ast}$ gives every point $m=y\,\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf a>0$. Where are such $\mathbf v$?

p01-feasible-c1.name: p01-feasible-c1
p01-feasible-c1.text: Each point restricts a half-plane. Points $(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$ need $-w_1>0$, that is $w_1<0$ (left of the purple line); points $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$ need $w_2>0$ (above the blue line).

p01-feasible-c2.name: p01-feasible-c2
p01-feasible-c2.text: The $\mathbf v$ satisfying both conditions form the green feasible region: $w_1<0$ and $w_2>0$.

p01-feasible-c3.name: p01-feasible-c3
p01-feasible-c3.text: Teaching-chosen $\mathbf v^{\ast}=(-1,2,0)$; the four points have $m$ equal to $1,2,2,1$, so $\gamma=\min m=1>0$.

p01-feasible-c4.name: p01-feasible-c4
p01-feasible-c4.text: $\mathbf v^{\ast}$ is only a "beacon" for the proof: the algorithm does not know where it is; only the proof needs it to exist.

p02-run-title.name: p02-run-title
p02-run-title.text: See an actual batch run: v walks step by step into the feasible region

p02-run-ctx.name: p02-run-ctx
p02-run-ctx.text: Start from $\mathbf v_0=(1,1,0)$ with learning rate $\rho=0.5$. Each step: find $Y$, sum $\mathbf s=\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$, update $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v+\rho\mathbf s$.

p02-run-src.name: p02-run-src
p02-run-src.text: Source: The steps follow KP02's batch update; the start $\mathbf v_0$ and $\rho=0.5$ are teaching choices, and $Y$ is empty after two updates (computed and checked by build_kp03_en.py).

p02-run-c0.name: p02-run-c0
p02-run-c0.text: The green region is feasible. The start $\mathbf v_0=(1,1)$ is outside. Where does $\mathbf v$ go with each update?

p02-run-c1.name: p02-run-c1
p02-run-c1.text: $m=-1,1,1,-1$: points $(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$ are wrong, $Y=\{z_1,z_4\}$. Total correction $\mathbf s_0=(-2,0,0)$.

p02-run-c2.name: p02-run-c2
p02-run-c2.text: $\mathbf v_1=\mathbf v_0+0.5\,\mathbf s_0=(0,1,0)$: exactly on the edge of the feasible region ($w_1=0$).

p02-run-c3.name: p02-run-c3
p02-run-c3.text: $Y$ is still $\{z_1,z_4\}$ and $\mathbf s_1$ has the same direction: $\mathbf v_2=(-1,1,0)$, inside the feasible region.

p02-run-c4.name: p02-run-c4
p02-run-c4.text: $Y$ is empty at $\mathbf v_2$, so we stop. Note $\mathbf v_2=(-1,1,0)$ differs from the chosen $\mathbf v^{\ast}=(-1,2,0)$: stopping only requires entering the feasible region, not hitting $\mathbf v^{\ast}$.

p03-two-facts-title.name: p03-two-facts-title
p03-two-facts-title.text: Two facts: s makes an acute angle with v* and an obtuse angle with the current v

p03-two-facts-ctx.name: p03-two-facts-ctx
p03-two-facts-ctx.text: Take the first update: $\mathbf v_0=(1,1,0)$, $\mathbf s_0=(-2,0,0)$. See the directions of $\mathbf v^{\ast}$, $\mathbf v_0$ and $\mathbf s_0$ (the $b$ component is 0, so we draw $w_1,w_2$).

p03-two-facts-src.name: p03-two-facts-src
p03-two-facts-src.text: Source: End of the KP03 lecture's "formal definition": $\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf s_t\ge\gamma$, $\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf s_t\le0$; the numbers are this page's main example.

p03-two-facts-c0.name: p03-two-facts-c0
p03-two-facts-c0.text: $\mathbf s=\sum_{i\in Y}y_i\mathbf a_i$ is the sum of all wrong points' requests. What angle does it make with $\mathbf v^{\ast}$, and with the current $\mathbf v$?

p03-two-facts-c1.name: p03-two-facts-c1
p03-two-facts-c1.text: Fact 1: every wrong point has $y_i\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf a_i\ge\gamma$; summing gives $\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf s\ge\gamma$. Here: $\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf s_0=2\ge1$, an acute angle.

p03-two-facts-c2.name: p03-two-facts-c2
p03-two-facts-c2.text: Fact 2: every wrong point has $y_i\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf a_i\le0$ (this is the definition of "wrong"); summing gives $\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf s\le0$. Here: $\mathbf v_0^T\mathbf s_0=-2$, an obtuse angle.

p03-two-facts-c3.name: p03-two-facts-c3
p03-two-facts-c3.text: Together: the direction of $\mathbf s$ points "toward the side of $\mathbf v^{\ast}$" and "away from the current $\mathbf v$". So each update brings us a bit closer in direction to $\mathbf v^{\ast}$.

p04-expand-title.name: p04-expand-title
p04-expand-title.text: Substitute the update into the "squared distance to αv*" and expand term by term

p04-expand-ctx.name: p04-expand-ctx
p04-expand-ctx.text: $D_t=\|\mathbf v_t-\alpha\mathbf v^{\ast}\|^2$: how far the current $\mathbf v$ is from "$\mathbf v^{\ast}$ scaled by $\alpha$". Take $\alpha=4$ here (the next page explains why).

p04-expand-src.name: p04-expand-src
p04-expand-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture §1.2 expansion; $\alpha=4=B^2/(2\gamma)$, where $B^2=8$ is the largest $\|\sum y\mathbf a\|^2$ over all non-empty subsets of the four points, enumerated by build_kp03_en.py.

p04-expand-c0.name: p04-expand-c0
p04-expand-c0.text: Substitute $\mathbf v_{t+1}=\mathbf v_t+\rho\mathbf s_t$: $D_{t+1}=\|\mathbf v_t-\alpha\mathbf v^{\ast}+\rho\mathbf s_t\|^2=D_t+\underbrace{2\rho\,\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf s_t}_{\text{term 1}}\;\underbrace{-\,2\rho\alpha\,\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf s_t}_{\text{term 2}}+\underbrace{\rho^2\|\mathbf s_t\|^2}_{\text{term 3}}$

p04-expand-c1.name: p04-expand-c1
p04-expand-c1.text: Term 1: $2\rho\,\mathbf v_0^T\mathbf s_0=2(0.5)(-2)=-2\le0$. Fact 2 keeps it from growing.

p04-expand-c2.name: p04-expand-c2
p04-expand-c2.text: Term 2: $-2\rho\alpha\,\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf s_0=-2(0.5)(4)(2)=-8$. Fact 1 makes it reduce by at least $2\rho\alpha\gamma$.

p04-expand-c3.name: p04-expand-c3
p04-expand-c3.text: Term 3: $\rho^2\|\mathbf s_0\|^2=0.25\times4=1$. The only term that increases, $\le\rho^2B^2$.

p04-expand-c4.name: p04-expand-c4
p04-expand-c4.text: All three together: $D_{t+1}\le D_t+\rho^2B^2-2\rho\alpha\gamma$. Here $D_0+B^2(\rho^2-\rho)=72\ge D_1=65$.

p05-contradiction-title.name: p05-contradiction-title
p05-contradiction-title.text: If it never stopped, the bound would fall below 0, but a distance is never negative

p05-contradiction-ctx.name: p05-contradiction-ctx
p05-contradiction-ctx.text: With $\alpha=B^2/(2\gamma)$ the inequality becomes $D_{t+1}\le D_0+B^2\bigl(\sum\rho_k^2-\sum\rho_k\bigr)$. Below is the lecture's scalar illustration: $D_0=8$, $B^2=2$, $\rho_k=1/(k+1)$.

p05-contradiction-src.name: p05-contradiction-src
p05-contradiction-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture §1.2 series illustration (not the four-point example); the table values for $t=5,20,80$ are wrong, so this is recomputed from the unrounded series.

p05-contradiction-c0.name: p05-contradiction-c0
p05-contradiction-c0.text: If the updates never stop, what happens to the upper bound $U_t$? Can it stay above 0 forever? (The red dashed line is 0.)

p05-contradiction-c1.name: p05-contradiction-c1
p05-contradiction-c1.text: $t$ up to 80: $U_0=8$, $U_2=7.0556$, $U_{20}=3.9061$, $U_{80}=1.3097$. Falling ever more slowly, still above 0.

p05-contradiction-c2.name: p05-contradiction-c2
p05-contradiction-c2.text: Going on, at $t=157$ we get $U_t=-0.0087<0$: $\sum\rho_k=\sum\tfrac1{k+1}$ (harmonic series) diverges and $\sum\rho_k^2$ converges (about 1.645), so it eventually wins.

p05-contradiction-c3.name: p05-contradiction-c3
p05-contradiction-c3.text: But $D_t=\|\cdot\|^2\ge0$ cannot be smaller than $U_t<0$. Contradiction: the assumption "updates never stop" fails.

p05-contradiction-c4.name: p05-contradiction-c4
p05-contradiction-c4.text: Conclusion: only finitely many updates happen, after which $Y$ is empty. Conditions needed: $\sum\rho_k=\infty$ and $\sum\rho_k^2<\infty$.

p06-fixed-step-title.name: p06-fixed-step-title
p06-fixed-step-title.text: A fixed learning rate also stops: pick a farther α so each update lowers D by at least ε

p06-fixed-step-ctx.name: p06-fixed-step-ctx
p06-fixed-step-ctx.text: The series condition is only sufficient. Fix $\rho=0.5$ and pick $\alpha=6>\rho B^2/(2\gamma)=2$: $\varepsilon=2\rho\alpha\gamma-\rho^2B^2$.

p06-fixed-step-src.name: p06-fixed-step-src
p06-fixed-step-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture §1.3; $\alpha=6$ for the four-point example is a teaching choice (any value above $\rho B^2/(2\gamma)$ works), and $D_t$ is recomputed from the actual run.

p06-fixed-step-c0.name: p06-fixed-step-c0
p06-fixed-step-c0.text: With $\alpha=6$, what are the actual $D_0,D_1,D_2$? How does each drop compare with $\varepsilon$?

p06-fixed-step-c1.name: p06-fixed-step-c1
p06-fixed-step-c1.text: Actual: $D_0=170$, $D_1=157$, $D_2=146$, dropping $13$ and $11$ each time, both larger than $\varepsilon$.

p06-fixed-step-c2.name: p06-fixed-step-c2
p06-fixed-step-c2.text: $\varepsilon=2(0.5)(6)(1)-0.25\times8=4$: every update is guaranteed to lower $D$ by at least $4$.

p06-fixed-step-c3.name: p06-fixed-step-c3
p06-fixed-step-c3.text: Even if each step lowers only $\varepsilon$, after $D_0/\varepsilon=42.5$ steps it would fall below 0. So at most $42$ updates can happen; more is a contradiction.

p06-fixed-step-c4.name: p06-fixed-step-c4
p06-fixed-step-c4.text: The bound is loose (only 2 updates actually happen), but it guarantees stopping in finitely many steps, and the step size does not need to shrink to 0.

p07-assumption-title.name: p07-assumption-title
p07-assumption-title.text: Premise: with non-separable data there is no v*, and the proof fails at step one

p07-assumption-ctx.name: p07-assumption-ctx
p07-assumption-ctx.text: A different data set: positive $(0,0),(1,1)$, negative $(0,1),(1,0)$ (XOR). Is there a line that separates them?

p07-assumption-src.name: p07-assumption-src
p07-assumption-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture "common myths": non-separable data has no strictly feasible $\mathbf v^{\ast}$; XOR is a standard counterexample chosen for teaching, not from the lecture.

p07-assumption-c0.name: p07-assumption-c0
p07-assumption-c0.text: Try drawing a line with the blue circles on one side and the red triangles on the other. We try three lines.

p07-assumption-c1.name: p07-assumption-c1
p07-assumption-c1.text: Line $x_1+x_2=0.5$: red triangle $(1,0)$ and blue circle $(1,1)$ land on the same side, one error.

p07-assumption-c2.name: p07-assumption-c2
p07-assumption-c2.text: Line $x_1=x_2$: both blue circles lie on the line, and whichever side we lean to, some point is wrong.

p07-assumption-c3.name: p07-assumption-c3
p07-assumption-c3.text: Line $x_1=0.5$: blue circle $(0,0)$ and red triangle $(0,1)$ are on the same side, another error.

p07-assumption-c4.name: p07-assumption-c4
p07-assumption-c4.text: No line separates XOR: there is no $\mathbf v^{\ast}$. The first step of the proof fails, and the perceptron may keep updating without stopping.

p07-assumption-c5.name: p07-assumption-c5
p07-assumption-c5.text: Conversely: not having stopped after long training does not prove the data is non-separable; it may simply not have trained enough.

p08-practice-title.name: p08-practice-title
p08-practice-title.text: Practice: which step sequences ρ_k = 1/(k+1)^a satisfy Σρ=∞ and Σρ²<∞?

p08-practice-ctx.name: p08-practice-ctx
p08-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: $\sum 1/k^p$ diverges for $p\le1$ and converges for $p>1$ (integral test). Four candidates: A $a=1$, B $a=0.5$, C $a=2$, D constant ($a=0$).

p08-practice-src.name: p08-practice-src
p08-practice-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture practice ($1/t$ versus $1/t^2$ series); A–D are new transfer cases; judgments follow the p-series, checked by check_numbers_kp03.py.

p08-practice-q.name: p08-practice-q
p08-practice-q.text: (a) Which satisfy both $\sum\rho_k=\infty$ and $\sum\rho_k^2<\infty$?  (b) Which condition does each of the others violate?  (c) Does D (constant step) lose its stopping guarantee?

p08-practice-a1.name: p08-practice-a1
p08-practice-a1.text: (a) Green zone $0.5<a\le1$: $\sum\rho=\sum k^{-a}=\infty$ ($a\le1$) and $\sum\rho^2=\sum k^{-2a}<\infty$ ($2a>1$). Only A.

p08-practice-a2.name: p08-practice-a2
p08-practice-a2.text: (b) B, D: $a\le0.5$, $\sum\rho^2=\infty$ (too large). C: $a>1$, $\sum\rho<\infty$ (too small, cannot get there).

p08-practice-a3.name: p08-practice-a3
p08-practice-a3.text: (c) No: a constant step does not satisfy the series condition, but the argument of §6 with a larger $\alpha$ still guarantees stopping in finitely many steps.

p09-summary-title.name: p09-summary-title
p09-summary-title.text: Summary: two facts, one expansion, one contradiction

p09-summary-ctx.name: p09-summary-ctx
p09-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the main example: the feasible region in the $\mathbf v$ plane, the update arrows and the upper bound of the distance.

p09-summary-e0.name: p09-summary-e0
p09-summary-e0.text: Premise: strictly separable data $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbf v^{\ast}$ exists, $\gamma=\min y\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf a>0$

p09-summary-e1.name: p09-summary-e1
p09-summary-e1.text: Two facts: $\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf s\ge\gamma$, $\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf s\le0$

p09-summary-e2.name: p09-summary-e2
p09-summary-e2.text: Expansion: $D_{t+1}\le D_t+\rho^2B^2-2\rho\alpha\gamma$; only the third term increases

p09-summary-e3.name: p09-summary-e3
p09-summary-e3.text: Contradiction: infinite updates make the bound negative but $D\ge0$. Conditions: $\sum\rho=\infty,\sum\rho^2<\infty$, or a fixed $\rho$ with a large $\alpha$

p09-summary-e4.name: p09-summary-e4
p09-summary-e4.text: Open question: must we sweep the whole batch before updating? Next KP: the online (per-sample) perceptron

p09-quantities-title.text: Three quantities for the proof: total correction $\mathbf s$, margin $\gamma$, maximum length $B^2$
p09-quantities-title.name: p09-quantities-title

p09-quantities-ctx.text: The four points of the KP03 main example ($\mathbf a$ ends in $1$) and the feasible $\mathbf v^*=(-1,2,0)^T$ are reused.
p09-quantities-ctx.name: p09-quantities-ctx

p09-quantities-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture §1 (definitions of $\mathbf s$, $\gamma$, $B^2$); $B^2$ comes from enumerating the $15$ nonempty subsets, recomputed independently. Added page: the original deck did not define $B^2$, restored from the lecture.
p09-quantities-src.name: p09-quantities-src

p09-quantities-hz.text: Each point requirement $\mathbf z_i=y_i\mathbf a_i$ and its component along $\mathbf v^*$
p09-quantities-hz.name: p09-quantities-hz

p09-quantities-c0.text: $\mathbf s_t=\sum_{i\in Y_t}y_i\mathbf a_i,\quad\gamma=\min_i y_i\mathbf v^{*T}\mathbf a_i>0,\quad B^2=\max_{\emptyset\ne S}\left\|\sum_{i\in S}y_i\mathbf a_i\right\|^2$
p09-quantities-c0.name: p09-quantities-c0

p09-quantities-c1.text: $\mathbf s_t$: the sum of the requirements of all misclassified points in this round. In the main example the first update has errors $z_1$, $z_4$, so $\mathbf s_0=\mathbf z_1+\mathbf z_4=(-2,0,0)$.
p09-quantities-c1.name: p09-quantities-c1

p09-quantities-c2.text: $\gamma$: the feasible $\mathbf v^*$ gives the four points labeled scores $1,2,2,1$, and the smallest is $\gamma=1$.
p09-quantities-c2.name: p09-quantities-c2

p09-quantities-c3.text: $B^2$: over any group of misclassified points, how large can the squared length of the summed requirements be? Listing the $15$ nonempty subsets: a single point gives $2$, all four points give $\mathbf s=(-2,2,0)$ and $8$, the largest, so $B^2=8$.
p09-quantities-c3.name: p09-quantities-c3

p09-quantities-c4.text: The two quantities each control one side: on the next page, expanding the squared distance after an update, $\gamma$ makes each update advance at least $2\rho\alpha\gamma$ along $\mathbf v^*$ (term 2), while $B^2$ caps the detour of one update at $\rho^2B^2$ (term 3).
p09-quantities-c4.name: p09-quantities-c4

p10-sequential-title.text: Going further: mistake bound for the one-at-a-time version, $M\le(R/\gamma_0)^2$
p10-sequential-title.name: p10-sequential-title

p10-sequential-ctx.text: Setup: $\mathbf z=y\mathbf a$, $\|\mathbf u\|=1$, $\mathbf u^T\mathbf z\ge\gamma_0>0$, $\|\mathbf z\|\le R$; $\mathbf v_0=\mathbf 0$ with fixed step $\rho$, fixing one misclassified point at a time ($\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf z\le0$).
p10-sequential-ctx.name: p10-sequential-ctx

p10-sequential-src.text: Source: KP03 lecture "going further" and [Added] example (plot uses $\rho=1$). Added page: the original deck left this out, restored from the lecture. This bounds the number of updates, not the batch formula.
p10-sequential-src.name: p10-sequential-src

p10-sequential-c0.text: After $M$ updates, how large can $M$ be? Squeeze with two inequalities: how long is $\mathbf v_M$ at least along $\mathbf u$, and how long is it at most?
p10-sequential-c0.name: p10-sequential-c0

p10-sequential-c1.text: Lower bound: each update adds $\rho\mathbf z$ and $\mathbf u^T\mathbf z\ge\gamma_0$, so $\mathbf u^T\mathbf v_M\ge M\rho\gamma_0$.
p10-sequential-c1.name: p10-sequential-c1

p10-sequential-c2.text: Upper bound: $\|\mathbf v_{t+1}\|^2=\|\mathbf v_t\|^2+2\rho\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf z+\rho^2\|\mathbf z\|^2\le\|\mathbf v_t\|^2+\rho^2R^2$ (on a mistake $\mathbf v_t^T\mathbf z\le0$). Summing gives $\|\mathbf v_M\|^2\le M\rho^2R^2$.
p10-sequential-c2.name: p10-sequential-c2

p10-sequential-c3.text: Squeeze: $M\rho\gamma_0\le\mathbf u^T\mathbf v_M\le\|\mathbf v_M\|\le\rho R\sqrt M$ (the middle step is Cauchy–Schwarz with $\|\mathbf u\|=1$). Cancelling $\rho$: $\sqrt M\le R/\gamma_0$, that is $M\le(R/\gamma_0)^2$.
p10-sequential-c3.name: p10-sequential-c3

p10-sequential-c4.text: Numeric example: the four points of KP04 with $\mathbf u=(-1,1,0)^T/\sqrt2$ give $\gamma_0=1/\sqrt2$, $R=\sqrt2$, so $M\le\left(\sqrt2/(1/\sqrt2)\right)^2=4$. Only $2$ fixes occur in practice; the bound need not be tight.
p10-sequential-c4.name: p10-sequential-c4

p10-sequential-c5.text: The bound is on the number of updates, not on sweeps, and it does not directly apply to the batch update. For non-separable data $\gamma_0$ does not exist and the proof premise fails.
p10-sequential-c5.name: p10-sequential-c5
